summary.text: For k>60, set \(n=2k+1\): any nonzero matrix entry directly gives two primes summing to \(2n=4k+2\), so if no such pair existed the whole matrix would be zero, contradicting its assumed nonzero determinant. The cases \(1\le k\le60\) are handled by an explicit finite list of prime decompositions.

full_proof.text:
Let \(A(n)\) denote the sequence A228623. Thus, for each positive integer \(n\), let \(M_n\) be the \(n\times n\) matrix whose rows and columns are indexed by \(0,1,\ldots,n-1\), and whose \((i,j)\)-entry is
\[
(M_n)_{i,j}=
\begin{cases}
1,&\text{if both }n+i-j\text{ and }n+j-i\text{ are prime},\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Then
\[
A(n)=\det(M_n).
\]
The expressions in the definition may be regarded as natural-number subtractions. There is no truncation for the allowed indices: if \(0\le i,j<n\), then \(j<n\le n+i\), so \(j\le n+i\), and similarly \(i\le n+j\). Consequently, these natural-number expressions agree with the corresponding integer differences.

Assume the conjectured nonvanishing property:
\[
\text{for every odd }n>120,\qquad A(n)\ne0.
\]
We prove that, for every positive integer \(k\), the integer \(4k+2\) is a sum of two primes.

Fix \(k>0\). We divide the proof into two cases.

### Case 1: \(k>60\)

Set
\[
n=2k+1.
\]
This integer is odd. Moreover, since \(k>60\), we have \(k\ge61\), and hence
\[
n=2k+1\ge123>120.
\]
The assumed nonvanishing property therefore gives
\[
A(n)=\det(M_n)\ne0.
\]

We claim that \(4k+2\) is a sum of two primes. Suppose, to the contrary, that no such pair of primes exists. Consider any indices \(i,j\) with
\[
0\le i<n,\qquad 0\le j<n.
\]
Put
\[
p=n+i-j,\qquad q=n+j-i.
\]
As noted above, because \(i,j<n\), both subtractions are exact rather than truncated. Therefore
\[
p+q=(n+i-j)+(n+j-i)=2n.
\]
Using \(n=2k+1\), this becomes
\[
p+q=2(2k+1)=4k+2.
\]
If the \((i,j)\)-entry of \(M_n\) were \(1\), then by the definition of the matrix both \(p\) and \(q\) would be prime. The displayed equality would then express \(4k+2\) as a sum of two primes, contrary to our supposition. Hence the \((i,j)\)-entry is \(0\).

Since \(i,j\) were arbitrary, every entry of \(M_n\) is zero. Thus \(M_n\) is the zero matrix. Also \(n=2k+1>0\), so this is a nonempty square matrix. Its determinant is zero: for example, every term in the usual permutation expansion of the determinant contains a zero matrix entry. It follows that
\[
A(n)=\det(M_n)=0,
\]
contradicting the previously obtained nonvanishing \(A(n)\ne0\). This contradiction proves that there do exist primes \(p,q\) such that
\[
4k+2=p+q
\]
whenever \(k>60\).

### Case 2: \(1\le k\le60\)

The remaining finite range is handled by explicit prime decompositions. The following table gives, for every \(k\) in this range, primes \(p,q\) satisfying \(p+q=4k+2\):

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c@{\qquad}c|c|c@{\qquad}c|c|c}
k&p&q&k&p&q&k&p&q\\ \hline
1&3&3&21&3&83&41&3&163\\
2&3&7&22&7&83&42&3&167\\
3&3&11&23&5&89&43&7&167\\
4&5&13&24&19&79&44&5&173\\
5&3&19&25&5&97&45&3&179\\
6&3&23&26&3&103&46&5&181\\
7&7&23&27&3&107&47&11&179\\
8&3&31&28&5&109&48&3&191\\
9&7&31&29&5&113&49&5&193\\
10&5&37&30&13&109&50&3&199\\
11&3&43&31&13&113&51&7&199\\
12&3&47&32&3&127&52&11&199\\
13&7&47&33&3&131&53&3&211\\
14&5&53&34&7&131&54&7&211\\
15&3&59&35&3&139&55&11&211\\
16&5&61&36&7&139&56&3&223\\
17&3&67&37&11&139&57&3&227\\
18&3&71&38&3&151&58&5&229\\
19&5&73&39&7&151&59&5&233\\
20&3&79&40&5&157&60&3&239
\end{array}
\]

For each row, direct addition gives \(p+q=4k+2\). All the displayed summands are prime. This can be checked by trial division: for each displayed number, it is enough to test the primes not exceeding its square root; the largest displayed summand is \(239\), whose square root is less than \(16\), so only divisibility by \(2,3,5,7,11,13\) can ever need to be checked. The entries \(2,3,5,7,11,13\) themselves are prime, and every larger displayed number has nonzero remainder upon division by every one of those primes that does not exceed its square root. Thus the table supplies the required prime pair in every case \(1\le k\le60\).

Combining the two cases, every positive integer \(k\) admits primes \(p,q\) with
\[
4k+2=p+q.
\]
Therefore the conjecture that \(A228623(n)\ne0\) for every odd \(n>120\) implies Goldbach's conjecture for all even integers of the form \(4k+2\) with \(k>0\).
